recommendations.regimenLabel: Stop culprit drug + burns-type supportive care
steps: STOP the culprit drug immediately (single most important step affecting outcome).
Manage like a burn — fluid/electrolyte balance, temperature control, meticulous wound/eye/mucosal care; ideally a burns/specialist unit.
Analgesia, nutrition, infection surveillance (avoid prophylactic antibiotics).
Ophthalmology and urology/gynae input for mucosal involvement; calculate SCORTEN.

drugRefs.dose: titrated to detached body-surface area, urine output and electrolytes (burn-type replacement)
drugRefs.why: Loss of skin barrier causes large fluid/electrolyte losses; volume requirements are usually lower than a comparable thermal burn but must be titrated to physiology.

refs: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 22e — Cutaneous Drug Reactions (Ch. 63)
UK Guidelines for the Management of Stevens-Johnson Syndrome/Toxic Epidermal Necrolysis in Adults (BAD)

drugRefs.dose: 3 mg/kg/day in two divided doses for ~7–10 days, then taper
drugRefs.why: Most-supported immunomodulatory agent in current SJS/TEN literature; given under specialist guidance.
Used in some protocols; evidence for benefit is mixed and it is given per specialist decision.
Emerging option with supportive trial data; specialist-directed, evidence evolving.

refs: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 22e — Cutaneous Drug Reactions (Ch. 63)

decision.label: Stop culprit drug; burns-unit supportive care

confirm: Painful mucocutaneous rash with blistering/skin detachment and mucosal erosions, usually drug-induced; SJS <10%, TEN >30% body-surface detachment.
